..

...Strong winds leading to critical fire weather conditions 
Saturday afternoon and evening...

Today and tonight: Fire weather concerns will be maximized this
afternoon and evening as a shortwave trough and dry cold front 
sweeps through the Pacific Northwest. A 99th percentile (around 
110 kt) upper level jet will be centered over north central 
Oregon to northeast Washington, setting the stage for 
unseasonably strong lee cyclogenesis in far southwest Alberta 
this afternoon. Mean sea level pressures will be around the 3rd 
to 5th percentile range for this time of year in southern BC and
southwest Alberta around 1000-1003 mb. This, along with higher 
pressure (1014-1016 mb) nosing into northwest Oregon and 
southwest Washington this afternoon will increase pressure 
gradients from southwest to northeast. The lower level response 
will be impressive as well with 700 mb winds around 30-50 kt and
850 mb winds around 25-35 kt (both solidly in the 99th 
percentile for this time of year). At the surface, much of the 
region can expect to see sustained southwest winds 15-30 mph 
with gusts around 25-45 mph this afternoon through this evening.
The areas of main concern for rapidly spreading fires will be 
the Columbia Basin, Waterville Plateau, Okanogan Valley, and the
West Plains where there is a 60-95 percent chance of wind gusts
exceeding 40 mph. Wind gusts peak around the 2-8 PM timeframe 
today. Wildfire smoke will be fairly extensive this afternoon as
the Little Giant Fire in Chelan County spreads smoke towards 
the Okanogan Valley, Highlands, and northern mountains. HRRR 
smoke runs also show plentiful mid to upper level smoke moving 
into eastern Washington and north Idaho. Wind speeds will slowly
decrease into the overnight hours as the boundary layer 
decouples but the midslopes and ridge tops of Selkirks and 
Cabinet/Purcell Mountains will remain quite windy gusting up to 
35 mph. There is a 10-20% chance of a light shower at the 
Cascade crest this evening. Rain amounts would be very light 
around a trace to 0.03 inches. 

Sunday and Monday: The overall pattern Sunday and Monday are 
fairly steady with longwave troughing continuing just offshore 
west-central British Columbia and strong high pressure centered 
over New Mexico. The Inland Northwest will stay in between the 2
systems, maximizing the thermal gradient aloft, which favors 
breezy conditions to continue. Fire weather conditions will be 
elevated to locally critical Sunday and Monday across portions 
of central and eastern Washington with south/southwest winds 
around 10-20 mph with gusts around 20-30 mph. The main area of 
concern will be the Okanogan Valley as diurnal upslope flow 
towards Canada will add onto the general winds. Any new or 
existing wildfires will be capable of rapid spread, especially 
the Okanogan Valley Sunday and Monday.

Tuesday: Fire weather concerns ramp back up Tuesday as models 
indicate a shortwave trough will sweep through Vancouver Island 
through south-central British Columbia. This will bring another 
dry cold front passage through the region. Central and Eastern 
Washington will be at most risk with southwest winds around 
15-25 mph with wind gusts around 20-35 mph. Relative humidity 
will remain low around 15-25 percent Tuesday afternoon and 
evening. 

Wednesday through Saturday: Temperatures will start to trend
upward towards the second half of next week as the southwestern
US ridge retrogrades westward towards Arizona and California and
strengthens. Temperatures Wednesday will be near average in the
80s and low 90s, but by Thursday and Friday, temperatures will
return into the 90s. Next Saturday/Sunday will need to be
monitored for fire weather as ensembles are generally in
agreement of troughing offshore British Columbia moving inland,
bringing in another dry cold front. Chances for rain in the next
week look bleak (near/at 0 percent chance) for the Inland
Northwest. /Butler
